name: Vasovagal / orthostatic syncope

matching.reasoningTemplate: Situational syncope with prodrome and rapid recovery, without cardiac features, suggests a vasovagal cause.

redFlags: Exertional or cardiac syncope needs cardiac workup

clinicalPearls: Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness from acute global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, brief duration, and spontaneous complete recovery; reorientation is almost immediate after a syncopal event.
Causes fall into three categories: neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac syncope; clinical features, mechanisms, and prognosis differ markedly among them.

Neurally mediated syncope is the most common cause overall in population-based studies and accounts for the vast majority of syncope in the young (peak incidence ~age 15); incidence is higher in women, and a first-degree family history is common in young patients.

Vasovagal syncope (the common faint) is provoked by intense emotion, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, and/or orthostatic stress; situational reflex syncopes have specific localized triggers (cough, micturition, swallow, defecation, carotid sinus pressure).
Premonitory (prodromal) features of autonomic activation in neurally mediated syncope include diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, hyperventilation, and yawning.
A functioning autonomic nervous system is required to develop neurally mediated syncope, in contrast to syncope from autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension).
Neurally mediated syncope can be subdivided by efferent pathway: vasodepressor (sympathetic vasoconstrictor failure), cardioinhibitory (bradycardia/asystole from vagal outflow), or mixed.

Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing or head-up tilt; supine and standing BP/HR at 3 min should be measured in every initial evaluation.
Initial clinical assessment plus ECG identifies a cause in about 50% of patients and stratifies cardiac mortality risk.
A clinically meaningful syncope usually corresponds to a fall in systolic BP to roughly 50 mmHg or lower; cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6-8 s produces loss of consciousness.
harrison.pathophysiology: Standing pools 500-1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities, buttocks, and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return, ventricular filling, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch trigger a compensatory reflex that raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal activity, increasing peripheral resistance, venous return, and cardiac output. In neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope this reflex transiently fails: there is a paroxysmal shift in autonomic efferent activity with increased parasympathetic outflow plus sympathoinhibition, producing bradycardia, vasodilation/loss of vasoconstrictor tone (vasodepressor response), and reduced cardiac output. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure drops cerebral blood flow below the limits of autoregulation, causing transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness. Multiple afferent triggers (orthostatic stress, carotid sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bladder) converge on the central autonomic network in the medulla. Hyperventilation-induced hypocarbia (cerebral vasoconstriction) and raised intrathoracic pressure (impaired venous return) contribute to many situational reflex syncopes. By contrast, orthostatic hypotension reflects chronic impairment of these homeostatic reflexes (autonomic failure), and cardiac syncope results from arrhythmias or structural disease reducing cardiac output.
additionalDifferentials: Generalized and partial/partial-complex seizures (with secondary generalization, usually preceded by an aura such as an unpleasant smell, fear, anxiety, or abdominal/visceral sensation).

Autonomic seizures (autonomic epilepsy), whose cardiovascular, GI, pulmonary, urogenital, pupillary, and cutaneous manifestations mimic syncopal prodrome; accompanying non-autonomic auras help distinguish them.
Hypoglycemia, typically in insulin-treated type 1 or type 2 diabetes (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias; hunger is not a typical syncope prodrome).
Cataplexy (abrupt loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger; consciousness is preserved, lasts 30 s to 2 min, no prodrome; occurs in 60-75% of narcolepsy).
Vertebrobasilar ischemia and hypoxemia as other causes of transient loss of consciousness.
Falls due to vestibular dysfunction, cerebellar disease, extrapyramidal/gait disorders, and falls with head trauma (especially difficult in patients with dementia and repeated falls).

Psychogenic apparent loss of consciousness from psychiatric disorders (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, major depression, somatization), suggested by frequent fainting without prodrome and rare injury despite numerous falls, with no significant hemodynamic change.
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG when arrhythmia or underlying cardiac disease is suspected; look for brady-/tachyarrhythmias, AV block, acute or old myocardial ischemia/infarction, long QT, and bundle branch block.
Supine and standing (3 min) blood pressure and heart rate to detect orthostatic hypotension.

Tilt-table testing (autonomic testing) to distinguish autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension from the hypotensive-bradycardic response of neurally mediated syncope, and to identify immediate or delayed orthostatic hypotension; may also reproduce psychogenic syncope when symptoms occur without hemodynamic change.

Autonomic function testing in specialized centers: heart rate variability to deep breathing and Valsalva (parasympathetic), thermoregulatory sweat test and quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (sympathetic cholinergic), and BP response to Valsalva/tilt (sympathetic adrenergic).

Carotid sinus massage (under continuous ECG and BP monitoring) for suspected carotid sinus syncope and in patients >40 years with recurrent unexplained syncope; avoid with carotid bruits, plaque, or stenosis.

Inpatient ECG monitoring for high arrhythmia risk; ambulatory Holter monitoring for frequent (near-daily) episodes; external or implantable loop recorders for less frequent episodes (monitor for at least twice the interspell interval).

Echocardiography for patients with cardiac history or abnormal exam/ECG (may reveal aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumors, aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade; also stratifies sudden-death risk by ejection fraction).
Treadmill exercise testing with ECG and BP monitoring for syncope during or shortly after exercise.
Invasive electrophysiologic studies (low sensitivity/specificity, rarely used) only when pretest probability is high in structural heart disease with ECG abnormalities.

Baseline blood tests are rarely helpful and should be reserved for suspected specific disorders (e.g., myocardial infarction, anemia, secondary autonomic failure); psychiatric screening for recurrent unexplained syncope.
redFlags: Syncope during exertion, or while seated or supine.
Sudden onset of palpitations immediately followed by syncope, or palpitations at the time of syncope.
Chest pain suggesting coronary ischemia, or features of congestive heart failure.
Moderate or severe valvular or structural cardiac disease, or known severe coronary artery disease.

ECG features: ischemia, history of ventricular arrhythmias, prolonged QT (>500 ms), repetitive SA block or sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, preexcitation, or a Brugada pattern.
New chest discomfort, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, or headache associated with the episode.
Exam: unexplained systolic BP <90 mmHg, signs of GI hemorrhage, persistent bradycardia <40 beats/min, or an undiagnosed systolic murmur.
harrison.prognosis: Syncope of noncardiac and unexplained origin in younger individuals carries an excellent prognosis with unaffected life expectancy. In contrast, cardiac syncope (structural heart disease or primary arrhythmia) is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and overall mortality, and mortality is also increased with orthostatic hypotension related to age and comorbidities. Hospitalization and mortality risk are higher in older adults.
pitfalls: Convulsive syncope mimics seizure: myoclonic and other movements occur in up to ~90% of syncopal episodes, but syncope-related jerks are typically arrhythmic, multifocal/generalized, and brief (<30 s), with mild flexor/extensor posturing; EEG seizure discharges are absent during syncope.

Distinguishing features from seizure: seizure loss of consciousness usually lasts >5 min with prolonged postictal drowsiness/disorientation, whereas reorientation after syncope is almost immediate; muscle aches are longer and more severe after seizures; seizures are rarely provoked by emotion or pain.
Urinary incontinence can occur in both syncope and seizure and does not distinguish them; fecal incontinence is very rare in syncope and postictal confusion is rare after syncope.
During neurally mediated syncope the eyes typically remain open and deviate upward with dilated pupils, and grunting/moaning/stertorous breathing may occur, which can be mistaken for a seizure.
Orthostatic hypotension syncope is usually preceded by warning symptoms but may occur suddenly, mimicking a seizure or cardiac cause.
Supine hypertension is common (>50%) in autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension; treating one condition can unmask or worsen the other.

Initial orthostatic hypotension (BP fall within 15 s, resolving by 45 s) and delayed orthostatic hypotension (beyond 3 min) can be missed by a single 3-min standing measurement; initial orthostatic hypotension does not represent autonomic failure.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison categorizes syncope by mechanism rather than a graded severity score: (1) neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, (2) orthostatic hypotension, and (3) cardiac syncope. For risk stratification, Table 23-1 lists high-risk features indicating hospitalization or intensive evaluation (e.g., ischemic chest pain, heart failure, significant valvular/structural disease, ECG ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia history, QT >500 ms, SA block/sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, family history of sudden death, preexcitation, Brugada pattern, palpitations at syncope, syncope at rest or during exercise). Neurally mediated efferent subtypes are vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory, and mixed.
